'''Dorothy Ann Eckels Bailie''' (born 1935) is an American mathematician who worked at [[Goddard Space Flight Center]] in the 1950s and 1960s. She was one of the three authors of the 1959 report establishing [[Figure of the Earth|Earth's shape]] as asymmetrical and "pear-shaped", based on data from [[Vanguard 1]].

== Early life ==
Dorothy Ann Eckels was born in [[Littleton, New Hampshire]] and raised in [[Laconia, New Hampshire]], the daughter of John C. Eckels and Dorothy R. Eckels.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|date=1959-11-05|title=William Bailie Takes Bride In New Hampshire Church|pages=40|work=Democrat and Chronicle|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86339443/william-bailie-takes-bride-in-new/|access-date=2021-10-02|via=Newspapers.com|archive-date=2021-10-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211002024213/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86339443/william-bailie-takes-bride-in-new/|url-status=live}}</ref> Her father was a surgeon. Her maternal grandfather, Adolph Frederick Erdmann, was a pioneer in the field of [[anesthesiology]].<ref>Erickson, James C. III. [https://www.woodlibrarymuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/history-of-anesthesia/in-the-beginning-adolph-frederick-erdmann-and-the-long-island-society-of-anesthetists.pdf "In the Beginning: Adolph Frederick Erdmann and the Long Island Society of Anesthetists"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211002024220/https://www.woodlibrarymuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/history-of-anesthesia/in-the-beginning-adolph-frederick-erdmann-and-the-long-island-society-of-anesthetists.pdf |date=2021-10-02 }} in Douglas R. Bacon, Kathryn E. McGoldrick, and Mark J. Lema. eds., ''The American Society of Anesthesiologists: A Century of Challenges and Progress'' (The Wood Library 2005): 1-8.</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Erdmann Certificate|url=https://www.woodlibrarymuseum.org/museum/erdmann-certificate/|access-date=2021-10-02|website=Wood Library-Museum of Anesthesiology|language=en-US|archive-date=2021-10-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211002024218/https://www.woodlibrarymuseum.org/museum/erdmann-certificate/|url-status=live}}</ref> She earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics at [[Middlebury College]] in 1957.<ref>{{Cite news|date=1959-02-06|title=Middlebury C. Woman Hit in Science Field|pages=13|work=Rutland Daily Herald|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86338249/middlebury-c-woman-hit-in-science-field/|access-date=2021-10-02|via=Newspapers.com|archive-date=2021-10-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211002024227/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86338249/middlebury-c-woman-hit-in-science-field/|url-status=live}}</ref> While at Middlebury, she was elected Queen of the school's Winter Carnival, an event she co-chaired.<ref>{{Cite news|date=1957-02-16|title=Middlebury Carnival Queen|pages=6|work=Rutland Daily Herald|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86340573/middlebury-carnival-queen/|access-date=2021-10-02|via=Newspapers.com|archive-date=2021-10-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211002024211/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86340573/middlebury-carnival-queen/|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Career ==
Bailie worked at the [[United States Naval Research Laboratory]] after college.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|date=1968-06-10|title=Mrs. Bailie Becomes First Alumna of Middlebury Phi Beta Kappa Unit|pages=4|work=The Burlington Free Press|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86338327/mrs-bailie-becomes-first-alumna-of/|access-date=2021-10-02|via=Newspapers.com|archive-date=2021-10-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211002024229/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86338327/mrs-bailie-becomes-first-alumna-of/|url-status=live}}</ref> By 1959 she worked in the Theoretical Division of [[NASA]]'s Goddard Space Flight Center, on calculating and analyzing complex orbits for satellites.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Binder|first=Otto O.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TaifDwAAQBAJ&dq=Ann+Eckels+Bailie&pg=PA90|title=Careers in Space|date=2019-06-28|publisher=Wildside Press LLC|isbn=978-1-4794-3929-4|pages=90|language=en}}</ref> She, R. Kenneth Squires, and [[John A. O'Keefe (astronomer)|John A. O'Keefe]] were the team that determined that the Earth was asymmetrical and "pear-shaped",<ref>{{Cite news|last=O'Keefe|first=John A.|date=1963-10-21|title=Our Pear-Shaped World|pages=14|work=Star Tribune|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86339143/our-pear-shaped-worldjohn-a-okeefe/|access-date=2021-10-02|via=Newspapers.com|archive-date=2021-10-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211002024217/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86339143/our-pear-shaped-worldjohn-a-okeefe/|url-status=live}}</ref> based on data from Vanguard 1.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=David|first1=Shayler|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pKENlNUWPEwC&dq=Ann+Eckels+Bailie&pg=PA104|title=Women in Space - Following Valentina|last2=Moule|first2=Ian A.|date=2006-08-29|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-1-84628-078-8|pages=104|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|date=April 1961|title=It's a Pear-Shaped World|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ptCxxK2RYdYC&dq=Ann+Bailie+Civil+Service&pg=RA3-PA20|journal=Civil Service Journal|volume=1|pages=20}}</ref>

[[James E. Webb]] mentioned Bailie, [[Nancy Roman]], and [[Eleanor C. Pressly]] in his 1961 commencement speech at [[George Washington University]], as examples of women in the space program.<ref>Wilds, Helen Elaine. [https://jewlscholar.mtsu.edu/bitstream/handle/mtsu/6145/Wilds_mtsu_0170N_11229.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y "Gendered Space: Emerging Frames in NASA Public Relations and Mainstream Media Representation, 1958-1966"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211002161008/https://jewlscholar.mtsu.edu/bitstream/handle/mtsu/6145/Wilds_mtsu_0170N_11229.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y |date=2021-10-02 }} (Master's thesis, 2019, Middle Tennessee State University): 80.</ref> In 1963, she was named one of the Ten Young Women of the Year by ''[[Mademoiselle (magazine)|Mademoiselle]]'' magazine.<ref>{{Cite news|date=1963-01-08|title=Student Journalist is Named One of 'The Ten Young Women of the Year'|pages=8|work=Redlands Daily Facts|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86338659/student-journalist-is-named-one-of-the/|access-date=2021-10-02|via=Newspapers.com|archive-date=2021-10-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211002024209/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86338659/student-journalist-is-named-one-of-the/|url-status=live}}</ref> Later in her career, she worked at [[Propellant depot|Analytical Mechanics Associates]] in Maryland.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">Jazwinski, Andrew H., Stanley F. Schmidt, Ann E. Bailie, and Norman Levine, [https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19680024358/downloads/19680024358.pdf "Suboptimal Filtering Part 4: Test Bed Computer Program"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211002161008/https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19680024358/downloads/19680024358.pdf |date=2021-10-02 }} (Analytical Mechanics Associates 1968).</ref>

== Personal life ==
Ann Eckels married accountant William J. Bailie in 1959.<ref name=":0" /> They had three children. Her husband died in 2009.<ref>{{Cite news|date=2009-03-16|title=William J. "Bill" Bailie|pages=C06|work=Hartford Courant|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86338987/william-j-bill-bailie/|access-date=2021-10-02|via=Newspapers.com|archive-date=2021-10-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211002024226/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/86338987/william-j-bill-bailie/|url-status=live}}</ref>
